exhibits.title: The Scales of Error
exhibits.text: A pair of scales that weigh a guess against the truth. The weight they report is the LOSS — a single number saying how wrong an answer is right now. Make that number small and the answer is good; that is the whole shape of learning from examples. The workhorse of these scales is MEAN SQUARED ERROR (MSE): take the difference between a prediction and its target, square it, and average over all the numbers involved. Squaring does two honest things at once — it makes every error positive, so overshoot and undershoot cannot cancel out, and it punishes large mistakes far more than small ones. It is the same 'sum of squares' that measures straight-line distance, so MSE is really just the squared L2 distance between what you predicted and what was true. Nothing here is specific to any one method: whenever you can say 'here is my guess, here is the right answer', these scales will tell you how far off you are, in one clean, differentiable number that something can then work to reduce.

exhibits.title: Why Squared
exhibits.text: Why square the error instead of taking its raw size? Three reasons. First, sign: squaring makes +2 and −2 both weigh 4, so overshoot and undershoot both count as wrong and cannot cancel when averaged. Second, emphasis: an error of 4 weighs 16 while an error of 1 weighs 1 — big mistakes dominate the bill, pushing whatever is being tuned to fix the worst errors first. Third, smoothness: the square has a clean, continuous slope everywhere (its derivative is simply 2 × error), which is exactly what a downhill search needs to follow. A worked weighing: if the true value is 0.4 and the prediction is 0.35, the loss is (0.4 − 0.35)² = 0.0025 — a tiny weight, a good guess. Compare that to a prediction of 0.9, which would weigh (0.4 − 0.9)² = 0.25, a hundred times heavier.

exhibits.title: Gradient Descent, Briefly
exhibits.text: A loss is only useful if you can reduce it. GRADIENT DESCENT is the method. The gradient is the direction in which the loss INCREASES most steeply as you nudge each adjustable number; so step a little in the OPPOSITE direction and the loss goes down. Repeat — new = old − (learning rate) × gradient — and you walk steadily downhill toward smaller error. The learning rate sets the stride: too large and you overshoot the valley and bounce; too small and you crawl. Backpropagation is just the efficient bookkeeping that computes this gradient through many chained steps at once. It is a patient, local procedure — feel the slope beneath your feet, take a small step down, feel again — and it is how essentially everything that learns from a loss is trained.

exhibits.title: Weigh, Square, Step Downhill
exhibits.spec:
graph LR
  P[prediction] --> D[difference vs target]
  T[target] --> D
  D --> S[square it → MSE loss]
  S --> G[gradient: slope of the loss]
  G --> U[step the knobs downhill]
  U --> P
exhibits.caption: Weigh the error, square it, follow the slope down, repeat — the loop beneath all learning from examples.

exhibits.title: The Parabola and the Walk Downhill
exhibits.caption: The left panel is the squared-error bowl, loss = (value minus target)-squared, with a walk downhill marked on it. From step 0 far up one wall, each step moves against the slope — new value = old minus (rate) times the gradient, and the gradient of a square is just 2 times the error. Notice the strides shrink as the wall flattens toward the minimum: the gentler the slope, the smaller the step, so the walk settles rather than overshoots. The right panel is why we square at all: it lays the raw size |error| beside error-squared. An error of 1 weighs 1 either way, but an error of 4 weighs 16 once squared — sixteen times heavier, not four. Squaring makes the largest mistakes dominate the bill, so the walk fixes them first.

exhibits.title: Where This Leads ↑
exhibits.text: These scales weigh far more than schoolbook fits. UP IN DIFFUSION: the ENTIRE training objective is one line on these scales — the squared difference between the true noise that was added and the noise the network predicted, ‖ε − net(x_t, t)‖². Because the noise used to corrupt an image is known, it doubles as the free answer key, and MSE does the rest. UP IN WORLD MODELS: the same squared distance is how I-JEPA scores a predicted representation against the true one, and how VICReg's 'invariance' term pulls two views together. Everywhere in the palace, when a model must be told how wrong it is, it is weighed on these scales — and gradient descent walks it downhill.
